1:
Henry reads the scene as an attack that misfires. The taunt was meant to frighten the king away from the LORD and instead frightens him toward him, as a wind that fails to strip a traveller's coat only makes him wrap it closer; the more the name is reproached the more the king studies to honour it. Calvin dwells on what it cost a monarch to make that turn, prostrating himself in filthy sackcloth after so many illustrious works, where scarcely one man in a hundred fails to murmur when God treats him with any severity. He adds the caution that ashes avail nothing without inward feeling, since hypocrites are always liberal with ceremonies. Ellicott marks the irony: at last the people did see their teacher, and the prophet they had derided was their one resource.

Calvin will not let the embassy be mistaken for a request to join in weeping. It was sent for consolation out of doctrine, since prayers poured into the air come to nothing if they do not rest on the word; he sets two remedies side by side, calling on God and consulting the prophets. He then raises the objection against his own king — was it distrust to ask a new promise from one already so furnished? — and answers that a man conscious of his weakness may seek fresh confirmations without shame, since the flesh keeps pulling toward distrust. He explains why the king sent rather than went, being at prayer in the temple, and observes that the prophet stayed at home not for ease but so that the king's faith might be tried by his absence.

The words of the message get close attention. Ellicott notes that the figure of children come to the birth without strength stands where a modern writer would use an adjective whose force he has half forgotten: every plan had literally miscarried. He hears in the plea for the remnant a word of the prophet's own lodged in the king's mind, and measures what was left by the invader's inscriptions, which count forty-six towns of Judah taken. Gill catches a smaller thing, that the king says thy God and not mine or ours, because he and his people were under chastening and undeserving of that relation.

Whether the perhaps of the fourth verse admits real doubt divides them. Calvin says it does not, arguing that believers often speak so when perplexed by a case though certain of the outcome, and comparing an apostle's if perhaps this thought may be forgiven thee, meant to strike the mind rather than leave the issue open. Gill reads it not as questioning but as hoping. Henry turns it into a rule, that the bare prospect of mercy should make us ply the oar of prayer with double diligence, prayer being the midwife of mercy and the children already at the birth.

The promise of a blast divides them again, and Clarke names an opponent. Secker had ruled that the phrase never means anything but putting a spirit into a person, here a spirit of deceit; Clarke does not think he has hit the true meaning and takes the word for a pestilential wind of the kind the Arabs call simoom, which he identifies outright with the angel who later smites the camp. Gill agrees that a plague-blast is meant. Ellicott goes the other way, preferring a spirit put into him, an impulse strong enough to overpower previous resolves, and warns that the received rendering wrongly suggests the calamity that came afterwards. Calvin rejects both the divine Spirit and the plague, taking a whirlwind that drives the invader off as easily as chaff. Ellicott adds that the rumour may be supernatural foresight or ordinary intelligence of an Ethiopian army on the move; Delitzsch records the return and the second attempt.
8:
Where the invader had gone, and what the envoy left, come by inference. Gill argues the army stayed before the city while its spokesman went back alone, since the letters that follow presuppose a siege still in place and would else have meant nothing. Clarke supposes the first siege was raised under pressure and a second town taken as easier. Ellicott notes both towns in the old allotment of Judah and thinks the move strategic, meant to intercept the Ethiopian advance, then stops honestly: some put the second in the Nile delta, and the narrative may suggest more than a shift between small forts, but in our ignorance of the ground nothing more can be settled. Calvin takes the Egyptian direction as probable, a camp moved to meet the armies early.

On the Ethiopian the readers pool what they have. Gill collects the name from Josephus, the Greek, Africanus and Strabo, and asks whether the country meant is upper Ethiopia beyond Egypt or the nearer one Bochart placed toward Midian. Ellicott is more precise, making him third of the Ethiopian dynasty whose founder had allied with the last king of Samaria, and citing an Assyrian inscription titling him king of Egypt and Ethiopia together. The counsellors had courted that alliance, and now, he observes, the army was moving. Calvin supplies the motive: two kings saw one power growing without limit, judged that separately they would be swallowed, and combined early.

Henry turns to what the king did not answer. No reply went back, because God had taken the work in hand; and the letter that came instead draws the observation that it is bad to talk proudly and profanely but worse to write so, since writing argues deliberation, spreads further and lasts longer. Spreading the sheet before the LORD he approves as letting it speak for itself. Clarke reaches for a modern parallel and finds a manifesto issued to the Parisians in 1792, forerunner of a torrent of blood, its author meeting a ruin he thinks nearly like this. He also makes the repeated verb in the ninth verse a copyist's echo, the true reading being he returned, which the Greek preserves and which yields the idiom he sent again. Delitzsch reads the sheets as one letter, not two.

The blasphemy holds Calvin. To call the author of truth a deceiver takes from God what is most absolutely his own, and the impiety had stayed hidden while its owner pretended to revere some deity. He mentions the conjecture that a traitor leaked the prophecy and sets it aside, since the promises were common talk and the people gloried in them openly. He then anatomises the boast: tyrants glory in ancestral crimes without asking whether the conquests were just, so the mightiest monarch is often best called the rich son of a great robber. Gill catches the letter's one courtesy, the title king of Judah, which the servant had refused.

The argument runs on two comparisons, as Calvin sets them out: this king against stronger predecessors who still fell, and the invader's house against the gods of the nations it had beaten. He answers pastorally — when the taunt is used against us, attend to the difference of condition. Ellicott identifies the places named: the first on the Khabur, the second the patriarch's resting place, the third between the Euphrates and Palmyra, the last a conqueror's renaming of the sort the annals record; the fathers of an eastern royal formula, he adds, are predecessors, not ancestors. Calvin places the first in Media and reports Pliny putting the second in Arabia against the general view, adding that historians who give it a plural name record Crassus dying there; Clarke notes its spelling in the manuscripts. Ellicott closes the roll grimly: the question once asked of the gods is now asked of their kings, and the answer is the dungeons of Nineveh.
14:
The spreading of the letter reads as a legal gesture. Ellicott calls it a mute appeal to the supreme arbiter, evidence laid before the judge before a word is spoken, and reports an Assyrian parallel: a king, receiving a defiant message from Elam, went into his goddess's temple, reminded her what he had done for her, and got an answer as a night vision. Calvin heads off the objection: the sheets are not opened because God needs informing, since he knows our wants before we ask, but because he lets us act so in accommodation to our weakness, and because it inflames the suppliant. Gill notices what the king did not do — no railing returned, no reply written, the letter left to be answered by the one it insulted. Clarke prefers the plural, read them and spread them, and puts the prayer in the sanctuary. Delitzsch, quoting only, marks where the prayer ends and the reply begins.

The titles opening the prayer are arguments, not ornament. Gill assigns each a use: the LORD of hosts is able, the God of Israel in covenant, the one above the mercy seat approachable. Ellicott hears the confession following as deliberate antithesis, an absolute monotheism set against the letter's polytheism. Calvin builds the clause into providence, since a God who rules every kingdom will not let a tyrant keep what he usurped; kings hold authority, he adds, by keeping the middle place between God and men and not wishing to climb higher.

Over the cherubim the readings part. Calvin rejects the view that they are simply angels, which would make the phrase mean God reigning in heaven among them, holding instead to the form of the ark, where the promise of presence attached. What he wants is a rule about nearness: the divine majesty exceeds heaven and earth and cannot be confined to our understanding, yet comes down in word and sign so feeble minds may climb by degrees, the sacraments serving as ladders that superstition turns the other way. Ellicott notes the same expression elsewhere describing storm clouds, and takes the reference here to be the glory-cloud between the ark's figures, themselves standing for the elemental powers of the sky.

The demand that God incline his ear troubles Calvin, who puts it as a question against himself: does the king suppose God asleep? No, but in a difficulty this size men speak as though he were absent, and what is asked is that help long held in hope become visible. He reads the prayer as evidence of the pressure, an earnestness breathing an amazing power of anguish, and turns it to instruction: the Lord wills that we toil and sweat and shiver, no victory won at rest. He also names what the king cared about most: not the kingdom but the name, since a city undertaken cannot be abandoned without its defender abandoning his honour.

The concession that follows is bounded. Ellicott observes that the facts of the boast are admitted and the inference alone denied, the cases not being parallel: those gods went into the fire, or to Nineveh as trophies, but one who has no graven image cannot. Calvin makes that distinction the beginning of piety, warning against men who rest in a dark speculation about some deity and cannot say whether they worship the God of the Turks or the Jews, touching neither heaven nor earth. His two arguments against the burnt gods are corruptible matter and human makers, with the flourish that the world's strength gathered into one man could not create a fig. Clarke works the text: the received word for lands destroys the sense, fifteen manuscripts and the parallel giving nations instead. Gill closes on the plea, covenant interest urged by one who knew a promise does not excuse asking. Calvin adds that those content with their own rescue put asunder what God joined.
21:
Ellicott opens with a chronological remark: on the corrected dating, the prophecy that follows is this prophet's last recorded utterance, so its contacts with his earlier work, and with the long poem traditionally ascribed to him, are worth watching. Henry observes that the answer came in writing, being too long for word of mouth, and that though the king might have been sent to an old prophecy for comfort, a message was made for him — the correspondence between earth and heaven is never let fall on God's side. Clarke notes that two versions take the verb passively, was sent, which Gill records and rejects as not agreeing with the Hebrew, and that the words I have heard have dropped out here, written above the line by a later hand in two manuscripts.

The taunt returned is put in the city's mouth. Ellicott sets it beside the same title used earlier of Zidon, where the virgin was ravished by invaders, and observes that this one was to escape the ravisher and laugh his lust to scorn. Calvin thinks addressing the whole church carries more force than addressing the king, heightening the baseness of scorning a defenceless people as if heaven's help counted for nothing; the city is an orphan insulted by a ruffian, and the father the insult strikes says he knows the schemes. Henry puts it briskly: the enemy may bark but cannot bite, and his threats are a mere flash without a bolt.

The repeated question about whom he reproached builds to its answer. Ellicott says the iteration exists to give the answer force, noting the irony that the title once sneered at was now the one deliverer. Clarke prefers against to the received to, on the parallel. Calvin turns the verse into a rule for the defenceless: having no armour and no advocate invites insolence, but those who fight us are at war with the living God, who has bound himself to hold all that is his and ours in common. He adds a portrait of the man in speech, face, gesture and eye, the sort who look down on everyone as if dropped from the sky.

That the reproach came through underlings aggravates it. Calvin notes it is harder to bear an insult from a servant than a master, and that proud men send a footman on purpose to make the contempt plainer. Gill adds that the master set his servants, and himself with them, above God. Clarke reads messengers rather than servants, corrects the height of his border to his lodge or retreat, the word for height having been caught by eye from a line above, and takes forest and fruitful field together as the whole country. Ellicott shows how conventional the boast was, quoting two Assyrian kings on trackless paths and rugged mountains unsuited to chariots, and doubts the range was crossed in this campaign: the phrase may have become a proverb for surmounting obstacles.

The boast about water divides on its object. Ellicott records that providing water was this king's pride, his inscriptions claiming wells dug in the desert, then argues the rivers he threatens to dry are Egypt's canals, since the word for that country also carries the sense of fortified enclosure; so read, the sentence defies the Ethiopian rather than Jerusalem. Delitzsch works the same wordplay and notes the perfects standing out against surrounding futures as statements of what actually happened. Clarke agrees on the canals and sets beside the boast a Latin poet's Alaric, who saw mountains sink under his feet and rivers dry, broke the Alps and ladled the Po with victorious helmets. Calvin keeps the threat local, reporting that some find the spring and cisterns of the besieged city here, and reading two clauses: the invader fears no drought since his numbers can dig, and expects to leave the city dry enough to kill by thirst.
26:
At this verse the speaker changes, as Ellicott notes, and the readers divide over what was done long ago. On the common view, held by Ellicott and Delitzsch, the invader's career had been planned and foreseen, his conquests a counsel he unwittingly served and not his own power; the events had lain in the divine mind as ideal before they were real, kings and armies being puppets in the drama, and the opening question assumes the Assyrian had heard these prophecies, likely enough in a court with ministers who knew Hebrew. Calvin says openly that the greater part of commentators read it so and that he explains it otherwise. On his account the thing made long ago is the city itself, named by a pronoun only, as though other cities counted for nothing, and the verse is a question — shall I now bring this to ruin, as I brought the rest?

What he wants from that reading is a doctrine of preservation. God founded the church and will not leave unfinished what he began, so its safety is his honour; and the making meant is not that of heaven and earth but the workmanship of a people created anew, a more excellent work, he says, than the whole creation. He sets the contrast boldly, asking where the majesty of Rome has gone and calling what survives of the world's mistress a workshop of iniquity. Fortified cities fall with their earthly strength; the church, small and feeble, rests on election and is renewed age by age through resurrections. He leaves the rabbis their dream that Jerusalem and the Messiah were made before the heavens.

The images of weakness that follow are handled textually. Ellicott would read and for therefore, notes one emblem of frailty following another with the housetop grass proverbial, and finds in the italics of the last clause a fault in transcription, the received words giving a field before the blades where the parallel gives a blasting. Clarke agrees, finding no authority for the word rendered parched and preferring blasted on six manuscripts; earlier he cut through two words he says embarrassed every interpreter, reading warlike nations for ruinous heaps with the Greek behind him. Gill notes that short of hand means the strength was taken away beforehand, which spoils the boast. Calvin works the housetop grass hardest: the higher it grows the nearer the heat and the sooner it withers, and no passer-by blesses it, so corn at our feet outvalues herbage on a roof.

The claim to know the man's sitting, going and coming is read as total. Ellicott observes that the three words are the ordinary Hebrew way of covering a whole life in its activity; Gill presses them into cabinet and camp. Calvin takes the first for deliberations and schemes, arguing that men may plan what they like against the church and accomplish nothing beyond permission, providence driving them so that they often reach, against their intention, a good end; while they storm on earth, heaven keeps a calm silence and laughs.

The metal in the nose gets the fullest annotation in the chapter. Clarke assembles it: the Aramaic version reads a ring, the iron one put through a camel's nostrils to check her restiveness, with the Talmudic ruling that she may go out on the sabbath wearing it; Jerome likewise has a ring. Ellicott notes that the Assyrian sculptures show beasts and men alike dragged so. Calvin argues for the ring against a hook, since hooks are for fish, and hears the sentence as pleasant mockery — gentleness gained nothing, so what cannot be tamed will be curbed; the retreat, he notes, would never have been chosen freely. Gill records one version reading the tumult as blasphemy, the noise that terrified the city being derided in heaven; Delitzsch calls the beast a lion led home by the nostril before reaching its goal.
30:
The address turns from invader to king, and the sign is agricultural. Gill notes the word can mean a wonder, this one no less marvellous than the deliverance it guaranteed. Ellicott dates the scene to autumn, near the equinox and so near a new year: tillage had stopped in spring, the coming year would live on what the fields threw up of themselves, and only in twelve months would the land be clear enough to sow. Delitzsch turns the dating into an argument. Thenius took the three years as the one just past, the one running, and the one to come; but so read, Delitzsch objects, nothing is signified, only a prediction that two bad years end in a third; it is a sign solely if the second year is still ahead.

Calvin raises another difficulty. There is an apparent impropriety, he says, in offering as a sign what happens only after the thing it confirms; a pledge ought to come first. His answer is that signs are of two kinds. Some go before and lead us to the event by the hand; others follow, to fix it deeply and keep it from being forgotten, as a people brought out of Egypt were told beforehand they would sacrifice three days after. Food was chosen, he adds, because famine follows war and wasted fields promise scarcity, so bread where none could be expected was the most convincing token, and kept the deliverance from seeming chance.

The promise to the survivors is an old word coming back. Ellicott recognises the remnant of the prophet's earliest formula and notes that the name given to a son long before was still an omen of good, the survivors a scion from which the future tree grows. Delitzsch says the watchword that a remnant shall return is now fulfilled, the spared city becoming the nation's source of renewal, and adds that the divine title here is missing from the parallel, being rare in that book. Calvin presses the smallness. Even with the siege lifted the people were few, fewer after the northern tribes were carried off, so the ground looked uprooted; but the church has a secret vigour that strikes root where none can be seen, and the lower her strength is brought, the surer we may be that God holds the means of multiplying a few.

Gill runs escaped forward to the elect, delivered not from the fall or corrupt nature but from justice, the law's curse and wrath to come. On the clause about zeal, Ellicott notes the prophet in old age returning to a formula of his early years and the promise once attached to it; Calvin makes it the answer to how so unlikely a thing could happen, God regarding his church with a love fervent enough to work outside the ordinary course. Delitzsch records that the definiteness of this closing section has been urged against its authorship, Hitzig calling it suspiciously precise, Knobel finding no reason to doubt the prophet wrote it.

What is promised is not that the city holds but that it is never attacked. Ellicott spells out the operations denied: advance under locked shields against missiles thrown by hand or engine, and earthworks raised to bring the assault up. The prediction, he stresses, is not only that the place will not fall, but that an enemy already encamped will not begin the usual works of a siege. Calvin differs on the last word, taking it for an engine that throws darts rather than a mound, since mounds are not poured. He orders the promises — enemy driven off, people fed, few made many — returning to the first because without it the rest count for nothing. Gill says the invader will lose his labour and make straight home; Calvin glosses the phrase by the common saying that a man returns as he came when nothing is done.
35:
The two reasons for the defence are weighed apart. Ellicott makes the first an assertion of majesty against blasphemy, the second a remembering of the promise, and draws from the pair a principle in the spirit of the second commandment: the good a man leaves survives as his evil does, so a later generation profits by its predecessor's virtue as it suffers for the guilt. Calvin agrees nothing in the people is in view, since they had provoked enough to deserve being abandoned. He then turns the clause against Rome: David is named for the promise and not the person, so the verse gives no footing to the intercession of saints and rather unsettles it. Gill hears only a shield, and asks who can hurt what God covers.

How the camp was destroyed is the largest question. Ellicott gives the modern answer: the words do not exclude, and he thinks imply, an epidemic spreading over days and brought to a head in one night. A history written now would dwell on the pestilence; to a prophet who saw winds as messengers it was simply the angel, and Ellicott sets beside it the wind that scattered the Armada and the frost that broke a march from Moscow. He reports too the Egyptian version from Herodotus, where a priest-king prayed and field mice gnawed the invaders' bowstrings at Pelusium. Some conclude the disaster fell in Egypt, not Jerusalem; Ellicott prefers writers with documents to the travellers' tales the vergers of Egyptian temples told the good Herodotus.

Calvin will have none of it. That part of the army died of plague in Egypt he calls an invention by which Satan, through profane historians, has darkened an extraordinary judgment, and objects on the numbers, since so many dying in a night cannot be pestilence; the father of lies, he says, has turned aside into Egypt a blessing given to the church. Other things he leaves open — whether the blow fell at the siege or on the march, whether by one angel or many, though he thinks one — and rejects a Jewish guess of thunder, since a thunderbolt would have been seen and reported.

The retreat is given three verbs, and both readers use them. Ellicott hears the proverbial phrase of a Roman orator for a man who left, escaped, broke away, and reconstructs the sequence: word of the pestilence in Egypt, a return to an army too weak to fight, a withdrawal abandoning the south. Calvin takes the repetition as mockery of a shameful flight, notes the royal title added to sharpen the disgrace, and observes that a man who settles at home has lost his nerve with his troops, since he would never have stayed quiet had despair not held him like a chain. Clarke recalls a prophecy of a people saved not by bow or sword but by their God; Delitzsch records the return and what followed in the temple.

On the murder the sources converge from opposite sides. Calvin, reasoning from character, says the ambition that reached for other men's lands could not keep peace at home, the plot growing from neglect of some sons and fondness for another; Ellicott, reasoning from a document, reports a will leaving the chief treasures and a new royal title to a seeming younger son, whose elder brothers revenged themselves on the father. Calvin adds that the killing was made as disgraceful as possible, not by a foreign enemy, not by rebels, not by servants, but by his own, and dismisses the tale that the king meant to sacrifice a son as Abraham did. On the god in whose house it happened Gill collects the guesses — a plank of the ark, Dagon, an Assyrian Belus dressed as Mars — while Ellicott reports the inscriptional identification disputed. Clarke ends where the chapter does: who can harden his neck against God and prosper?
